summary: A legendary child of immense strength associated with the Ashigara mountain region and later traditions of Sakata no Kintoki.
description: Institutional records connect Kintarō with the Ashigara mountain region and with the later warrior identity Sakata no Kintoki. The archive treats these as evolving narrative associations rather than a single recoverable biography.
traditionNotes: Japan Search distinguishes early references to a Yorimitsu retainer from early-modern expansions of the Kintarō childhood story.

variants.label: Child hero and warrior retainer
variants.description: The mountain child and the adult retainer are linked in later narrative tradition, while source histories and dates remain layered and uncertain.

sourceNotes: Japanese spellings and romanization are checked against the NDL authority record; narrative summary is kept deliberately narrow.

summary: A mountain-woman figure whose representations range across threatening, maternal, and theatrical traditions.
description: One prominent Edo-period visual tradition pairs Yamauba with Kintarō. The Metropolitan Museum of Art identifies an Utamaro print from about 1795 in which the pair are presented as adoptive mother and son.
traditionNotes: This record does not treat a single print or maternal interpretation as the totality of Yamauba traditions.

variants.label: Maternal pairing with Kintarō
variants.description: Utamaro produced multiple images of Yamauba and Kintarō, including intimate mother-and-son scenes.

sourceNotes: The visible record is an artwork-grounded entry, not a complete survey of Yamauba scholarship.

summary: The broad mountain region traditionally associated with Kintarō, near the modern Kanagawa–Shizuoka border.
description: Japan Search describes Ashigarayama as a mountainous region associated with Kintarō and situates that tradition around the border of present-day Kanagawa and Shizuoka prefectures.
traditionNotes: The archive maps Ashigara as an approximate traditional region rather than asserting one exact legendary coordinate.

variants.label: Region rather than point
variants.description: Ashigarayama can refer to a broad mountainous setting; later Kintoki naming adds another layer of place association.

sourceNotes: Geographic certainty is intentionally shown as approximate/traditional.

summary: A jewel motif within Buddhist visual culture, often represented as a flaming or wish-granting jewel.
description: The British Museum records a 1905 collaborative Japanese painting of sixty-four hōju and describes them as wish-granting or lucky jewels in a Buddhist visual context.
traditionNotes: The broad Buddhist motif and the ASHIGARA relic are related visually but are not identical claims.

variants.label: Flaming and lucky jewel forms
variants.description: Institutional cataloguing connects hōju with flaming-jewel and lucky-jewel iconography across different works.
variants.period: Long visual history; cited example from 1905

sourceNotes: This is a concise object-motif entry; broader doctrinal interpretation requires specialist review.

summary: An oni leader at the center of a famous demon-slaying tale associated with Minamoto no Yorimitsu and his retainers.
description: Tokyo National Museum presents the Shuten-dōji tale as a long-lived subject of illustrated storytelling. A British Museum Ibuki-dōji handscroll preserves a materially different birth-and-upbringing variant tied to Mount Ibuki and Mount Ōe.
traditionNotes: Settings, origin episodes, spellings, and details change across texts and images; this record foregrounds that variance.

variants.label: Ibuki-dōji handscroll
variants.description: A British Museum handscroll centers birth and upbringing at Mount Ibuki before movement to Mount Ōe.

sourceNotes: The page does not collapse the Ibuki and Ōe settings into one supposedly definitive version.

summary: A Heian-period warrior transformed by later tales and images into a central demon-slaying hero.
description: Institutional exhibitions connect Yorimitsu and his retainers with the Shuten-dōji and Tsuchigumo story cycles. The archive distinguishes the historical person from legendary narrative roles.
traditionNotes: Raikō is an on-reading of the same name; the stories displayed here belong to later narrative and visual traditions.

variants.label: Warrior and legendary demon slayer
